tagline: A prophetic vision given to John on Patmos, showing the slain and risen Lamb on the throne behind history and the renewal of all things.
overview:
Revelation is the last book of the Bible and one of its most vivid. Its title comes from its first word in Greek, apokalypsis, an unveiling. John, exiled on the island of Patmos, sees the risen Jesus standing among lampstands and receives messages for seven churches in the Roman province of Asia. Then a door opens in heaven, and John is shown God's throne, a scroll sealed with seven seals, and a Lamb who was slain yet stands. What follows is a sequence of visions: seals opened, trumpets blown, bowls poured out; a dragon, two beasts, a great prostitute called Babylon; the fall of that city, the return of Christ, a thousand-year reign, the final judgment, and at last a new heaven and a new earth, where God dwells with his people and wipes every tear from their eyes.

The book was written to real churches under real pressure. Some were being slandered and imprisoned; others were comfortable and compromised, tempted to make peace with the idolatry and commerce of Rome. Revelation shows them the world as heaven sees it: the empire that seems eternal is a beast that will fall, and the Lamb who was killed is the one who rules. Its call is to faithful witness, to endurance, and to refusing the worship the world demands.

Few books have been read in more ways. It has comforted martyrs, inspired hymns and art, and been used to predict dates that came and went. Reading it well means taking seriously both its first readers and its promise that the whole creation will be made new.
author: The author names himself four times simply as John (1:1, 1:4, 1:9, 22:8), a servant of God, a brother and companion in suffering, and a prophet. He doesn't call himself an apostle. From the second century, writers such as Justin Martyr and Irenaeus identified him with John the apostle, the son of Zebedee. In the third century, Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, argued from differences in Greek style and vocabulary that Revelation's author was not the writer of the Gospel of John, though he accepted that the author was a holy man named John. The debate continues. Many scholars today speak of John the prophet or John the seer, a Christian prophet well known to the churches of Asia, possibly the same as or distinct from the apostle. Others defend apostolic authorship, explaining the rougher Greek by the book's genre, its heavy use of Hebrew idiom, or the circumstances of exile. The deep links in theme and imagery with John's Gospel (Jesus as the Word, the Lamb, living water, the one who was pierced) are acknowledged on all sides.
date:
Two main dates are proposed. The majority view places Revelation late in the reign of the emperor Domitian (AD 81 to 96), around AD 95. This rests largely on Irenaeus, who wrote about AD 180 that the vision was seen near the end of Domitian's reign, and on details in the book that seem to fit that time: developed imperial worship in Asia, churches that have had time to decline from their first love (2:4), and the figure of a returning Nero, which may echo legends that circulated after Nero's death.

A significant minority dates the book to the late 60s, under or just after Nero (AD 54 to 68), who persecuted Christians in Rome after the great fire of AD 64. Supporters point to the measuring of the temple in chapter 11, which could suggest it was still standing before its destruction in AD 70, to the count of kings in 17:9-11, and to the observation that the number 666 matches the name Nero Caesar written in Hebrew letters. The variant 616, found in the papyrus P115 from Oxyrhynchus and in Codex Ephraemi and already known to Irenaeus, matches the Latin spelling of the same name and strengthens the Nero reading. The date matters for interpretation, especially for readings that see much of the book fulfilled in the first century.
setting:
John writes from Patmos, a small rocky island in the Aegean Sea off the coast of Asia Minor, where he says he was because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus (1:9). Most interpreters take this to mean exile or banishment, a punishment Roman authorities used for troublesome figures. The seven churches he addresses lay in cities of the Roman province of Asia (western Turkey today), roughly in a loop along a road from the coast inland: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea. These were prosperous Greek cities, proud of their temples, games, trade guilds, and loyalty to Rome.

That loyalty was expressed through the imperial cult, the worship of the emperors and of the goddess Roma alongside the traditional gods. Cities competed for the honor of building temples to the emperors. Participation in civic festivals, guild banquets, and trade often involved sacrifice and food offered to idols. For Christians, refusing could mean losing business, social standing, or safety. Jewish communities, whose ancestral religion was recognized, sometimes clashed with the Christian groups in their cities. Whether Domitian mounted an organized, empire-wide persecution is doubted by many historians; the pressures Revelation describes may have been mostly local, social, and economic, with violence breaking out at points, as with Antipas in Pergamum (2:13).
purpose: Revelation was written to strengthen persecuted believers and to wake up complacent ones. It unmasks the powers of the world, showing that behind the glamour of empire stand a dragon and a beast, and it reveals that God reigns and the Lamb has already conquered by his death. It calls the churches to repent where they have compromised, to endure where they are suffering, and to overcome as the Lamb overcame, by faithful witness even to death. And it gives them a destination: the new Jerusalem, where God's presence fills everything.
story: Revelation is the last act of the Bible's story and draws its threads together. The tree of life, lost in Genesis 3, stands again in the city of God (22:2). The garden becomes a city, and the temple becomes the whole of creation filled with God's presence. The promises to Abraham of a people from every nation, to David of an everlasting king, and through the prophets of a new creation meet here. The book is saturated with the Old Testament, especially Daniel, Ezekiel, Isaiah, Zechariah, and Exodus, though it rarely quotes directly. The story that began with God creating the heavens and the earth ends with God making all things new.
christ: Revelation is, as its first line says, the revelation of Jesus Christ. He appears as the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth (1:5), as the glorious Son of Man among the lampstands, and above all as the Lamb who was slain. The central vision of chapter 5 shows the Lion of the tribe of Judah, and John looks and sees a slaughtered Lamb standing on the throne. That reversal defines the book: Christ conquers by sacrifice. He receives the same worship as God, bears titles given to God (the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last), rides out as the faithful and true Word of God, and at the end is the bridegroom of his people and the lamp of the new city.
reading:
Revelation belongs to several genres at once. It is an apocalypse, a type of Jewish and Christian writing that uses symbolic visions, heavenly guides, numbers, and cosmic imagery to reveal the hidden meaning of history (Daniel 7-12 is the Bible's other major example). It is a prophecy, calling for response. And it is a letter, addressed to seven real churches. The symbols are meant to be understood, often by reference to the Old Testament, and numbers like seven, twelve, and a thousand usually carry meaning rather than serving as a code for calculation.

Interpreters have followed four main approaches. Preterists read most of the book as fulfilled in the first centuries, in the fall of Jerusalem or of pagan Rome. Historicists read it as a map of church history from John's day to the end. Futurists read most of chapters 4 to 22 as events still to come before Christ's return. Idealists read it as a portrayal of timeless realities, the ongoing conflict between God and evil in every age; this approach goes back to Tyconius, a fourth-century North African whose reading shaped Augustine's view that the book's visions repeat the same age from different angles (recapitulation). Many readers combine them.

The thousand years of chapter 20 divide readers too. Premillennialists expect Christ to return before an earthly thousand-year reign; this includes historic premillennialism and dispensational premillennialism, which usually adds a rapture of the church before a seven-year tribulation. Postmillennialists expect the gospel to bring a long age of flourishing before Christ returns. Amillennialists read the thousand years as the present age of Christ's reign between his first and second comings. Faithful Christians hold each of these views. The book's own interest is less in timetables than in worship, endurance, and hope.

structure.title: Prologue and vision of the Son of Man
structure.summary: John introduces the book, greets the seven churches, and sees the risen Christ among seven lampstands, who commissions him to write.

structure.title: Messages to the seven churches
structure.summary: Christ addresses each church in Asia with praise, rebuke, warning, and a promise to the one who overcomes.

structure.title: Throne, scroll, seals, and trumpets
structure.summary: John sees God's throne and the slain Lamb who opens the sealed scroll. Seals and trumpets bring judgments, interludes show the sealed people of God and the faithful witnesses, and the seventh trumpet announces the kingdom.

structure.title: The dragon, the beasts, and the Lamb's people
structure.summary: The conflict behind history is shown: the dragon wars against the woman and her children, the beasts demand worship, and the Lamb stands with his people on Mount Zion.

structure.title: Bowls of wrath and the fall of Babylon
structure.summary: The last plagues are poured out, Babylon the great is judged and mourned, heaven rejoices, and Christ rides out to defeat the beast.

structure.title: The thousand years, judgment, and new creation
structure.summary: Satan is bound, the dead are judged, and John sees the new heaven and new earth and the holy city, where God dwells with his people. The book closes with the promise of Christ's coming.

themes.title: God reigns
themes.body: The throne is the book's central image. Whatever chaos appears on earth, the vision of chapter 4 shows the One seated on the throne, worshiped day and night. History is not out of control, and the empires that claim ultimate power are not ultimate.

themes.title: The Lamb who conquers by dying
themes.body: Christ's victory comes through his death, and his people share it the same way. They overcome by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony. Revelation redefines power and victory around the cross.

themes.title: Worship and idolatry
themes.body: The book is full of songs sung in heaven, and its great conflict is over who will be worshiped: God and the Lamb, or the dragon and the beast. Idolatry in Revelation is political and economic as well as religious, bound up with empire and trade.

themes.title: Faithful witness and endurance
themes.body: The Greek word for witness, martys, gives us the word martyr. Jesus is the faithful witness, Antipas is called his faithful witness, and the churches are called to bear witness even at cost. Endurance, not escape, is the characteristic virtue of the saints in this book.

themes.title: Judgment and new creation
themes.body: Revelation does not flinch from judgment on evil, but it does not end there. The goal is a renewed creation in which God dwells with his people, death is gone, and the nations walk in the light of the Lamb.

keyChapters.why: John's commission on Patmos and the vision of the risen Christ among the lampstands, the First and the Last who holds the keys of death.
The first four messages to the churches, showing Christ's intimate knowledge of real congregations and his call to overcome.
The Lion who is a slain Lamb takes the scroll, and all creation worships him: the theological heart of the book.
The dragon's war against the woman and her child shows the spiritual conflict behind history.
The beasts from the sea and the land, the demand for worship, and the number 666.
The binding of Satan, the thousand-year reign, and the final judgment, the source of the millennial debates.
The new heaven and new earth and the holy city, where God dwells with his people and makes all things new.
The river and tree of life, and the closing promise and prayer for Christ's coming.

parts.body:
Revelation is the last book of the Bible, twenty-two chapters, and it can be read aloud in about an hour and a quarter. Its title comes from its first word in Greek, apokalupsis, an unveiling: “This is the revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave Him to show His servants what must soon come to pass” (1:1). It pulls back a curtain so that its readers can see their world as heaven sees it.

A man named John, on the small island of Patmos, sees the risen Jesus standing among seven golden lampstands. Jesus gives him messages for seven churches in the Roman province of Asia, in what is now western Turkey (chapters 2 and 3). Then a door opens in heaven. John sees God's throne, and a scroll sealed with seven seals that no one can open, until a Lamb who had been slain, yet stands, takes it (chapters 4 and 5). What follows is a series of visions: seals opened, trumpets blown, bowls poured out; a dragon, two beasts, a great city called Babylon; the fall of that city, the coming of Christ, a thousand years, the last judgment, and at last ‘a new heaven and a new earth’, where God lives with his people and wipes every tear from their eyes (21:1-4).

The book was written to real churches under real pressure. Some were poor, slandered and in danger. Others were comfortable and tempted to make peace with the idols and the trade of their cities. Revelation shows them that the empire which seemed to last forever was not the last word, and that the Lamb who was killed is the one who reigns. Its call is to faithful witness, to endurance, and to refusing the worship the world demands.

Few books have been read in more ways. It has comforted martyrs and given the church some of its greatest songs. It has also been used again and again to set dates for the end, and every one of those dates has passed. These notes set out the main ways Christians read it, each as its holders would put it, and they choose none. They give no scheme of the last days and no date, and they identify no nation, leader, church or event of our own time with any figure in the book.

The book opens with a blessing: “Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear and obey what is written in it” (1:3). It was meant to be heard, understood and kept.

The writer names himself four times, simply as John (1:1, 4, 9; 22:8). He calls himself God's servant, ‘your brother and partner in the tribulation’ (1:9), and a prophet. He does not call himself an apostle. That is what the book itself shows: a Christian prophet named John, well known to the churches of Asia, sharing their hardships.

From the second century, writers such as Justin Martyr and Irenaeus identified him with John the apostle, the son of Zebedee. In the third century, Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, compared the Greek of Revelation with the Gospel of John and argued that they could not be by the same writer, though he accepted that the author was a holy man named John.

The debate continues. Many scholars today speak of John the prophet or John the seer, who may be the same as the apostle or may be another John. Others hold that the apostle wrote it, and explain the rougher Greek by the kind of book it is, its heavy use of Hebrew ways of speaking, or the conditions of exile. On all sides, readers notice the deep links of theme and picture with John's Gospel: Jesus as the Word, the Lamb, living water, the one who was pierced.

So the honest answer has two parts. What is known: the writer was a Christian prophet named John, writing to the seven churches from Patmos. What is not known for certain: whether he was the apostle John. These notes do not choose.

The church received Revelation unevenly. The Muratorian list, usually dated to the late second century, includes it. In parts of the Greek East it was doubted for a long time. Eusebius, in the early 300s, said it could be placed among the acknowledged books or among the rejected, depending on the reader's judgment. The Syriac churches long read a New Testament without it, and it is still not read in the Orthodox liturgy. In the end the whole church received it as Scripture.

Two main dates are proposed. Most scholars place Revelation late in the reign of the emperor Domitian, who ruled from AD 81 to 96, around AD 95. This rests largely on Irenaeus, who wrote about AD 180 that the vision was seen near the end of Domitian's reign, and on details in the book that seem to fit that time: worship of the emperors well established in Asia, and churches that have had time to grow cold (2:4).

A significant minority dates it to the late 60s, under or just after Nero, who ruled from AD 54 to 68 and persecuted Christians in Rome after the great fire of AD 64. They point to the measuring of the temple in chapter 11, which could suggest it was still standing before AD 70, to the count of kings in 17:9-11, and to the number 666, which matches the name ‘Nero Caesar’ written in Hebrew letters. These notes do not choose. The date matters most for readings that see much of the book fulfilled in the first century.

The seven churches lay in cities of the Roman province of Asia, roughly in a loop along a road from the coast inland: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea (1:11). These were proud, prosperous Greek cities, with temples, games, trade guilds and loyalty to Rome. That loyalty was shown through the worship of the emperors and of the goddess Roma beside the old gods. Trade guilds held banquets in honour of their gods, and civic festivals involved sacrifice. For a Christian, refusing could mean losing business, standing or safety.

Whether Domitian led an organised, empire-wide persecution is doubted by many historians. The pressures Revelation describes may have been mostly local, social and economic, with violence breaking out at times, as with ‘My faithful witness Antipas’, who ‘was killed among you’ (2:13).

parts.h: What kind of book it is
parts.body:
Revelation belongs to three kinds of writing at once, and it names all three in its opening verses.

It is an apocalypse (1:1). That is the name scholars give to a family of Jewish and Christian books, written roughly between 250 BC and AD 250, in which a seer receives visions, often explained by an angel, that show the hidden reality of heaven and the true meaning of history. Daniel 7 to 12 is the Bible's other great example. These books speak in symbols: beasts stand for kingdoms, horns for rulers, numbers for qualities.

It is a prophecy (1:3). It is a word from God that calls for a response now.

And it is a letter (1:4), sent to seven real churches, meant to be read aloud in each of them.

That has some plain consequences for reading. The symbols are meant to be understood, and the book often explains its own: “The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches” (1:20). Where it does not explain, the first place to look is the Old Testament, which Revelation echoes constantly; scholars count several hundred allusions, though it rarely quotes word for word. Daniel, Ezekiel, Isaiah, Zechariah, Exodus and the Psalms are everywhere.

Numbers usually carry meaning rather than serve as a code for working things out. Seven stands for completeness, twelve for God's people, a thousand for a great and complete number. Revelation often hears one thing and then sees another, and the second explains the first. In chapter 5 John hears of ‘the Lion of the tribe of Judah’ who has triumphed, and turns to see “a Lamb who appeared to have been slain, standing in the center of the throne” (5:5-6). The conquering king conquers by being slain. That reversal is the key to the whole book.

Unlike Daniel, who was told to seal up his book until the time of the end (Daniel 12:4), John is told, “Do not seal up the words of prophecy in this book, because the time is near” (22:10). Revelation was meant to be opened and understood by its first hearers.

The risen Christ and the seven churches (chapters 1 to 3). John on Patmos; the vision of Christ among the lampstands; a message to each church, with praise, rebuke and a promise ‘to the one who overcomes’.

The throne, the Lamb and the scroll (chapters 4 and 5). Heaven's worship of the Creator, and the slain Lamb who alone is worthy to open the scroll.

Seals and trumpets (chapters 6 to 11). Two series of seven judgments. Between them come pauses that show God's people sealed and kept, and two faithful witnesses. The seventh trumpet announces that ‘the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ’ (11:15).

The conflict behind history (chapters 12 to 14). A dragon wars against a woman and her child; a beast from the sea and a beast from the land demand worship; the Lamb stands with his people on Mount Zion.

The bowls and the fall of Babylon (chapters 15 to 19). The last series of judgments; the great city judged and mourned; heaven's song; Christ rides out as ‘Faithful and True’.

The thousand years, the judgment and the new creation (chapters 20 to 22). Satan bound; the dead judged; a new heaven and a new earth; the holy city, the river and the tree of life; and the closing promise, ‘I am coming soon’.

Notice the series of sevens. Readers differ on whether the seals, trumpets and bowls follow one another in time, or tell the same story more than once from different angles, each time pressing closer to the end. That question is part of the larger question of how to read the book.

Christians have read Revelation in four main ways, usually called preterist, historicist, futurist and idealist. They differ mainly over when the events of chapters 4 to 22 take place. Each has a long history, and each has been held by serious and faithful interpreters. Here each is set out as its holders would put it. These notes do not choose.

The preterist reading (from the Latin for ‘past’) holds that most of the book's prophecies were fulfilled in the first centuries, in the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, or in God's judgment on persecuting Rome, or both. Its holders say that Revelation spoke to its first readers about what was about to happen to them, as its repeated ‘soon’ and ‘the time is near’ suggest (1:1, 3; 22:10). Partial preterists hold that the return of Christ, the resurrection and the last judgment are still to come. A small number go further and hold that the second coming and the resurrection happened in AD 70; nearly all churches reject that view, because the creeds confess a future return of Christ and resurrection of the body.

The historicist reading holds that Revelation is a prophetic outline of the whole history of the church, from John's day to the end, with its seals, trumpets and bowls matching events one after another down the centuries. It was the main Protestant reading from the Reformation to the 1800s, and some churches still hold it. Historicist readers have often matched the book's figures with particular rulers, churches and events of their own times. These notes make no such match.

The futurist reading holds that after the letters to the seven churches, most of the book (chapters 4 to 22) describes events still to come, in a time of great trouble just before Christ returns. Its holders point out that early writers such as Justin Martyr and Irenaeus expected a future Antichrist and a future kingdom. In the 1800s one form of futurism was joined to dispensational teaching, with a rapture of the church before the time of trouble; other futurists, such as George Eldon Ladd, hold a future reading without that rapture.

The idealist reading, sometimes called the spiritual or symbolic reading, holds that Revelation does not map particular events, but shows in pictures the conflict between God and evil, the church and the world, which is repeated in every age until Christ returns and ends it. Its roots are in Tyconius, a North African writer of the late 300s, and in Augustine, who read the thousand years as the present age of the church. Its holders say the book speaks to every generation of believers alike.

Many recent commentators combine these approaches. They read the book as addressed first to the seven churches under Rome, as showing patterns that recur through the church's history, and as looking ahead to a real return of Christ, last judgment and new creation.

Whatever reading a person holds, one thing is plain from the book's history. Confident readings that tied a beast or a horn to a ruler of their own day have come and gone in every generation. These notes identify no nation, leader, church, movement or event of our own time with any figure in Revelation, and they set no date. Jesus said, “No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father” (Matthew 24:36).

Revelation 20 says that Satan is bound for a thousand years, and that those who had been faithful to death “came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years” (20:4). It is the only place in the Bible that speaks of a thousand-year reign, and Christians have held several main views of it. It is a question that divides faithful churches, not the faith; it has never divided the church's creeds. Here each view is set out as its holders would put it. These notes do not choose.

Amillennialists hold that the thousand years is a picture of the present age between Christ's two comings. Christ reigns now from heaven; Satan is bound so that the gospel reaches the nations (Matthew 12:29); the faithful dead live and reign with Christ. Revelation's visions repeat the same age from different angles, so chapter 20 does not follow chapter 19 in time. The return of Christ is one event, followed at once by the resurrection of all, the judgment and the new creation. They note that this reading, shaped by Tyconius and Augustine, has been the majority view of the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Reformed traditions.

Postmillennialists hold that Christ will return after a long age in which the gospel, through ordinary preaching and the work of the Spirit, brings the nations broadly under his rule. They point to Jesus' parables of the mustard seed and the leaven, which picture the kingdom growing until it fills the world (Matthew 13:31-33). They say this is not confidence in human nature but in the power of God. The view was held by many Puritans, by Jonathan Edwards and by B. B. Warfield, and it gave confidence to much of the missionary movement of the 1700s and 1800s.

Historic premillennialists hold that Christ will return before a thousand-year reign on the earth, and that the church will pass through the final time of trouble rather than be taken out of it. They read Revelation 20 in the order it gives: the faithful come to life and reign, and the rest of the dead do not come to life until the thousand years are over. They note that this was the hope of Papias, Justin and Irenaeus before Augustine. George Eldon Ladd gave the view its modern scholarly form.

Dispensational premillennialists hold that God's promises to the nation of Israel still stand and will be kept to the letter. Christ will first come for his church in a rapture (1 Thessalonians 4:17), which most in this tradition place before a seven-year time of trouble drawn from Daniel 9; then Christ will return openly with his saints and reign from Jerusalem for a thousand years, before a final rebellion, the last judgment and the new creation. Its holders say this is what a consistent reading of prophecy requires, and that it honours God's faithfulness to every promise. The system was shaped by John Nelson Darby and spread by C. I. Scofield; some in it place the rapture in the middle of the time of trouble or before the outpouring of God's wrath.

All these views agree on what the creeds confess. Christ ‘shall come again, with glory, to judge both the quick and the dead’, as the Nicene Creed says. The dead will be raised, and God will make all things new. Faithful Christians hold each view, and they are brothers and sisters. Revelation's own interest is less in the order of events than in worship, endurance and hope.

Revelation is, as its first line says, ‘the revelation of Jesus Christ’. Its centre is a picture. In chapter 5 no one in heaven or on earth can open the scroll of God's purposes, and John weeps. Then he is told that the Lion of the tribe of Judah has triumphed. He looks, and sees a Lamb that had been slain, standing at the centre of the throne. Christ conquers by sacrifice. And his people conquer the same way: “They have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony” (12:11).

Jesus is ‘the faithful witness, the firstborn from the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth’ (1:5). He receives the same worship as God. He takes God's own titles: ‘the Alpha and the Omega’, ‘the First and the Last’ (1:8, 17; 22:13). He holds ‘the keys of Death and of Hades’ (1:18). He rides out as ‘Faithful and True’, and ‘His name is The Word of God’ (19:11-13). And at the end he is the bridegroom of his people, and ‘the Lamb is its lamp’ in the holy city (21:23).

The worship of heaven fills the book. The living creatures never stop saying, “Holy, Holy, Holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come” (4:8). The new song to the Lamb says, “by Your blood You purchased for God those from every tribe and tongue and people and nation” (5:9). The great conflict of the book is over worship: God and the Lamb, or the dragon and the beast.

The seven messages in chapters 2 and 3 are the only parts of the book addressed to named congregations, and they anchor everything that follows in real places and real struggles. Each follows a pattern: a title of Christ from the vision of chapter 1; ‘I know your deeds’; praise, rebuke or both; a call to repent or hold fast; a promise to ‘the one who overcomes’; and the refrain, ‘He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.’ That refrain shows that every church was meant to hear every message.

Two churches, Smyrna and Philadelphia, receive no rebuke. Both are small and under pressure. The two most sharply warned, Sardis and Laodicea, seem the most comfortable. Christ judges by what he sees, not by how a church sees itself.

Some phrases in these chapters need care. ‘The synagogue of Satan’ (2:9; 3:9) speaks of a local conflict in two cities in the first century. It is never a statement about the Jewish people, and the notes on those chapters say so plainly. ‘The Nicolaitans’ (2:6, 15) are otherwise unknown. ‘Jezebel’ (2:20) is Christ's name for a false prophetess at Thyatira, drawn from Ahab's queen in Kings; it is not a label for any woman or group today. And the promise to Philadelphia to be kept ‘from the hour of testing’ (3:10) is read in more than one way in the debate over the rapture; the note on 3:7-13 sets out the views.

Revelation was written to people who were suffering, or about to. John calls himself their ‘partner in the tribulation and kingdom and perseverance’ (1:9). In Smyrna believers were poor and slandered, and some were about to be thrown into prison (2:9-10). In Pergamum Antipas had been killed (2:13). Under the altar in heaven John sees those who had been killed for their witness, and hears them cry out, ‘How long?’ (6:10).

The book does not tell them that their suffering is a punishment. It tells them that God sees it, that their cry is heard, and that the one who was slain is on the throne. It calls them to endure, not to escape. The Greek word for witness, martus, later came to mean a martyr, and Revelation is one reason why.

It also promises an end. “‘He will wipe away every tear from their eyes,’ and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the former things have passed away” (21:4).

Not every hardship comes from following Jesus, and not every hardship is meant to be endured in silence. If you are carrying something heavy, whether persecution, illness, loss, or harm at the hands of others, it is right to seek help and safety. Please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. If you are in danger, or the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

Many readers are troubled by Revelation's pictures of judgment: plagues, war, a city burned. Those pictures are real parts of the book, and they should not be smoothed away. But a few things help in reading them.

They are pictures, drawn largely from the Old Testament, from the plagues of Egypt and the prophets' oracles against proud cities. They show that evil will not have the last word, and that God will judge it. For people who were being crushed by an empire, that was not a threat but a hope.

They are not commands to God's people to fight. In Revelation, believers overcome by faithful witness and by the blood of the Lamb, not by the sword. Christ's own sword comes ‘from His mouth’ (1:16; 19:15): his word.

And judgment is not the end. The goal is a renewed creation. “Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth” (21:1). God's dwelling is with his people. The river of life flows from the throne, and the leaves of the tree of life are ‘for the healing of the nations’ (22:2). The story that began in a garden ends in a garden city.

Christians differ over how the final judgment works and what it involves; the doctrine studies on judgment and on hell set out the views.

Revelation almost never quotes the Old Testament word for word, but it echoes it on nearly every page.

The Son of Man among the lampstands comes from Daniel: “I saw One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven” (Daniel 7:13). The cry of the living creatures echoes the seraphim of Isaiah: “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts” (Isaiah 6:3). The plagues of trumpets and bowls echo the plagues of Egypt. The people of God as ‘a kingdom, priests’ (1:6) recalls Sinai: “unto Me you shall be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:6). The pierced one whom all will see comes from Zechariah: “they will look on Me, the One they have pierced” (Zechariah 12:10).

And the end of the book gathers up the prophets' hope. “For behold, I will create new heavens and a new earth” (Isaiah 65:17). “The Lord GOD will wipe away the tears from every face” (Isaiah 25:8). The tree of life, lost in Genesis 3, stands again by the river of the city (22:2). The kingdom Daniel saw, which “will never be destroyed” (Daniel 2:44), has come.

It is not a timetable. It sets no date, and these notes set none. Many dates have been set from it, and every one has passed.

It is not a code for reading the news. These notes identify no nation, leader, church, movement or event of our own time with any figure in the book.

It is not a book meant to frighten. It was written to give endurance and hope to people who were suffering, and it begins and ends with a blessing.

It is not a call to violence. Its people overcome by faithful witness and the blood of the Lamb.

And it is not only about the future. Every message to the seven churches spoke to their present, and every vision asked them how to live now.

Read it aloud if you can, as it was meant to be heard. Read chapters 1 to 5 first, slowly; everything after rests on the vision of Christ, the seven churches, the throne and the Lamb.

Look for the book's own explanations of its symbols, and look to the Old Testament for the rest. Treat numbers as pictures first.

Notice the songs. Much of Revelation is worship, and the worship scenes are its heart.

Read it with the seven churches in mind. Ask what each vision meant to a small church in Smyrna or Laodicea before you ask what it means for anyone else.

Where readers differ, on how to read the book, on the thousand years, on the rapture, read more than one view before you settle, and hold your own view as one who may yet be taught. Be humble about particular identifications.

And let it end where it ends, with a prayer: “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus” (22:20).

The notes on each chapter go through it passage by passage in plain words.

Sunday, the day of the resurrection (1:10).

Greek metanoeō, to change mind and direction (2:5).
Christ, slain and standing at the centre of the throne (5:6).

timeline.what: Pergamum receives the first temple in Asia to Augustus and Roma.
A great earthquake strikes Sardis, Philadelphia and other cities of the region.
An earthquake strikes Laodicea, which rebuilds from its own wealth.
The great fire of Rome; Nero blames the Christians.
The Romans destroy Jerusalem and its temple.
The date given by a significant minority for the book.
The date most scholars give, following Irenaeus.
Irenaeus writes that John saw the vision near the end of Domitian's reign.
Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, is burned to death there.
Dionysius of Alexandria argues that the writer of Revelation was not the writer of John's Gospel.
Eusebius is undecided whether Revelation belongs among the acknowledged books.
Tyconius reads the book spiritually; Augustine reads the thousand years as the church's present age.

places.name: Ephesus
places.line: The first church addressed, in the greatest city of the province of Asia, famous for its temple of Artemis. Doctrinally careful, it had left its first love (2:1-7).

places.name: Laodicea
places.line: The last church addressed, in a wealthy city of the Lycus valley, known for banking, black wool and medicine. Christ calls it lukewarm, and knocks at its door (3:14-22).

teaching.mapNote: Revelation names Patmos and seven cities of the Roman province of Asia (1:9, 11). The site's maps so far have checked points for only two of them, Ephesus and Laodicea, so only those are drawn. Smyrna lay north of Ephesus, Pergamum further north, Thyatira, Sardis and Philadelphia inland, and Laodicea about a hundred miles east of Ephesus.
